clue.text: What it takes to become a churchwarden

definitions.text: What it takes to become a churchwarden

parts.words: What it takes to become a churchwarden
parts.note: the surface suggests the qualifications for a parish office, but a churchwarden is also a long-stemmed clay tobacco pipe, and this asks what material such a pipe is made from

explanation.surface: Someone asks what qualifies a parishioner to be elected churchwarden.
explanation.walkthrough: A churchwarden is an old-fashioned tobacco pipe with a very long stem, moulded from fine white clay.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine white clay is the material from which long tobacco pipes such as the churchwarden were moulded.

clue.text: Quiet watercourses to the mills or folds

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for playing quietly
a leat is an open channel carrying water to a mill wheel

explanation.surface: Someone describes calm streams leading to mill buildings, or else creases in fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: A leat is a mainly British term for the man-made channel that feeds a watermill.
explanation.definitionFit: Folds pressed into cloth, as in a skirt, are synonyms here.

clue.text: Such things can be most absorbing

definitions.text: Such things can be most absorbing

parts.words: Such things can be most absorbing
parts.note: absorbing sounds like gripping or fascinating, but here it means literally soaking up liquid, as a sponge does

explanation.surface: A remark that some pursuits can be utterly engrossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absorbing' suggests interest; the clue means things full of tiny holes that soak up water.
explanation.definitionFit: Materials full of tiny holes let liquid soak in, which is the literal sense of absorbing.

clue.text: Abdicate position as King of the Castle

definitions.text: Abdicate position as King of the Castle

parts.words: Abdicate position as King of the Castle
parts.note: King of the Castle is a children's game of standing on a mound; giving up that perch means literally descending, and the phrase also means backing down in an argument

explanation.surface: A monarch gives up his throne and fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: King of the Castle is a playground game where one child holds the top of a mound against the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Retreating from a stated stance is an idiom for conceding, and literally the game's king steps off his heap.

clue.text: It's a case of being completely taken in

definitions.text: It's a case of being completely taken in

parts.words: It's a case of being completely taken in
parts.note: taken in suggests being fooled, but here it means absorbed and incorporated wholly into something larger

explanation.surface: Someone describes having been thoroughly duped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' reads as deceived; the clue means absorbed, like food by the body or immigrants by a culture.
explanation.definitionFit: Absorption of something so that it becomes part of the whole is the process meant.

clue.text: Flower akin to London Pride?

parts.note: London Pride is a garden plant, so a flower seems meant, but flower is crossword slang for a river, something that flows, and London takes pride in its river

explanation.surface: A gardener asks which bloom is related to the saxifrage called London Pride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a crossword convention for river; London Pride is a pink saxifrage and also a famous London beer.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river running through the capital is something Londoners are proud of, and a river flows.

clue.text: They have every prospect of succeeding

definitions.text: They have every prospect of succeeding

parts.words: They have every prospect of succeeding
parts.note: succeeding sounds like achieving success, but it means following someone into a title or estate

explanation.surface: A forecast that some promising candidates are bound to do well.
explanation.definitionFit: Those next in line to inherit are expected to take over a title or property when the holder dies.

clue.text: Strictly speaking, it's what he's expected to be

definitions.text: Strictly speaking, it's what he's expected to be

parts.words: Strictly speaking, it's what he's expected to be
parts.note: strictly speaking looks like a hedging phrase, but read literally it says someone who speaks strictly, a stern disciplinarian

explanation.surface: A pedantic aside about what a man is really supposed to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strictly speaking' normally means 'to be precise'; here it describes a person who gives orders strictly.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigid disciplinarian insists on strict obedience to rules.

clue.text: Odd way to estrange a policeman, for instance

indicators.note: an odd way of arranging something means its letters are put in an unusual new order

explanation.surface: A complaint about a strange method of alienating a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd way to' is the anagram signal: rearrange the letters of ESTRANGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A police officer may hold this rank, above constable, so he is one example of it.

clue.text: Nothing comes before this

parts.note: reads like praise for a top priority, but it literally describes whatever is first in time

explanation.surface: Someone declares that something is their absolute top priority.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of early names the point in time before which there is nothing else.

clue.text: Fairy-tale beauty judge apparently changing sides

definitions.text: Fairy-tale beauty judge apparently changing sides

parts.words: Fairy-tale beauty judge apparently changing sides
parts.note: in Snow White the wicked queen asks a magic glass who is fairest of all, and a looking glass swaps left and right

explanation.surface: The judge of a fairy-tale beauty contest seems to switch allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing sides' suggests a turncoat; it refers to a reflection reversing left and right.
explanation.definitionFit: A looking glass judged beauty in Snow White, and any reflecting glass swaps left for right.

clue.text: Rustic merry-making — in a hop-garden?

parts.note: hop is both a plant grown in Kentish gardens and an informal dance, so a hop in the fields suggests rural folk dancing

explanation.surface: A rural celebration held among the hop plants of a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A hop-garden is a field where hops for beer are grown; a hop is also an informal dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional folk dancing in rural areas, often in rows or sets, is this kind of festivity.

clue.text: Lift operator of a sort!

parts.note: a lift operator sounds like someone running an elevator, but a hitch-hiker gets a lift by sticking out a digit

explanation.surface: Someone describes an unusual kind of elevator attendant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' means an elevator in Britain, but here it is a free ride, which a hitch-hiker requests with a raised digit.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitch-hikers signal for a ride by holding out this digit, so it secures them a free journey.

clue.text: Light drink? Nonsense!

definitions.meaning: the glow of the night sky's satellite

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of a low-alcohol beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions run together: the light from the moon, bootleg whisky, and foolish talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunar glow, bootleg liquor and foolish talk are three separate meanings of one word.

clue.text: Where Jack is the centre of attraction

definitions.text: Where Jack is the centre of attraction

parts.words: Where Jack is the centre of attraction
parts.note: Jack seems to be a person in the limelight, but the jack is the small white ball that players aim at in bowls

explanation.surface: A place where a man named Jack is the star of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: In the game of bowls, players roll their balls as close as they can to a small target ball called the jack.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn bowls is played on this kind of flat turf, with every bowl aimed at the jack.

clue.text: Happy one tops the list up in the Colosseum

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on top of another means it comes first

parts.note: glad means happy
the Roman numeral I is one

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a rota is a list of duties

explanation.surface: A cheerful winner heads the league table at the ancient Roman arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns ROTA into ATOR, and 'tops' puts GLAD and I above it in this down entry. The definition is loose: a fighter found in the Colosseum.
explanation.definitionFit: Armed fighters battled in the Roman arena, so such a combatant is what one would find there.

clue.text: Solidly built, but a bone-headed lot

definitions.meaning: a group of stupid people, taking thick as dim and set as a group

explanation.surface: A description of burly people who are not very bright.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: thick means stupid, and a set is a group.
explanation.definitionFit: Stocky describes a sturdy frame, and dim plus group gives the split reading.

clue.text: Antony said it should be made of sterner stuff

definitions.text: Antony said it should be made of sterner stuff

parts.words: Antony said it should be made of sterner stuff
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Mark Antony's funeral speech says of Caesar's alleged vice that it should be made of sterner stuff

explanation.surface: A quotation from Mark Antony about something needing more toughness.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Julius Caesar, Act 3: Antony argues Caesar wept for the poor, and the fault he was accused of should be made of sterner stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's alleged vice in Antony's speech was the drive for power and advancement.

clue.text: Mad Maria in a hunt for a benevolent man

indicators.note: mad signals that the following letters are scrambled into a crazy new order

explanation.surface: A frantic woman named Maria searches for a kind-hearted man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' is the anagram signal for MARIA IN A HUNT, twelve letters that rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A philanthropist who works to improve people's welfare is a kindly person of this type.

clue.text: Stick with present company

indicators.note: with here means the two pieces are put alongside each other

parts.note: here means present, as when answering a roll call

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to stay loyal to the people around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a noun but is the verb: hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: To bond or hold together firmly is to adhere.

clue.text: The way to get around or through the mountains

definitions.meaning: a road that avoids a town centre
split as two words, by meaning via and a pass being a mountain gap

explanation.surface: Directions offering a road that goes either round the range or across it.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word into two: by (via) and pass (a gap through mountains).
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road that skirts a town is one meaning; via a mountain gap is the split reading.

clue.text: 9 days

parts.note: the number points to the answer of 9 across, and the solver must think of the period of life those days describe

explanation.surface: A bare reference to a span of nine days.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is a cross-reference to 9 across, so read the clue as 'earliest days' of a life.
explanation.definitionFit: The first years of a person's life are their youngest days, the period of being young.

clue.text: Material appropriate for the barrack-square

definitions.meaning: the parade-ground marching practice that soldiers do on a barrack-square

explanation.surface: Someone picks out cloth suitable for a military parade ground.
explanation.walkthrough: A barrack-square is the parade ground of an army base, where soldiers practise marching.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy twill cotton is one sense; marching practice for soldiers is the other.

clue.text: Not what the White Tower was made of

definitions.text: Not what the White Tower was made of

parts.words: Not what the White Tower was made of
parts.note: the White Tower is the stone keep of the Tower of London, unlike the proverbial tower of academic seclusion named after an elephant-tusk material

explanation.surface: A historical note about the building material of the Tower of London's keep.
explanation.walkthrough: The White Tower is the Norman keep of the Tower of London, built of stone; the phrase 'ivory tower' means a retreat from real life.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant tusk is white, so a white tower might be thought made of it, as in the idiom for a sheltered retreat.

clue.text: Some duty-free perhaps one's taken in return journeys

indicators.note: taken in means the letter is placed inside the other piece
return means the word for journeys is read backwards

parts.note: trips are journeys
the Roman numeral I is one, with 's meaning 'is'

explanation.surface: A traveller buys duty-free goods on the way home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns TRIPS into SPIRT, and 'taken in' puts I inside it. Duty-free shops sell spirits such as whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits like gin or whisky are a typical airport duty-free purchase, an example of what is sold there.

clue.text: Hate a man possibly expressed in a curse

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters are one of several possible arrangements

explanation.surface: Someone voices loathing for a man by swearing at him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' signals an anagram of HATE A MAN; 'expressed in' only links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal ecclesiastical curse or banning is the original sense, now anything detested.

clue.text: Sound as a bell

parts.note: the phrase normally means perfectly healthy, but here it asks for the noise a small bell makes

explanation.surface: A declaration that something is in perfect condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound as a bell' is an idiom for fit and well; read literally it is the noise of a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A light ringing chime is the noise a little bell makes.

clue.text: Don't look so closely without a match

definitions.meaning: split as two words, peer meaning look closely and less meaning not so much

explanation.surface: Advice to stop squinting, and a remark about lacking a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word: peer (look closely) plus less.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrivalled describes something with no equal, and the split reading is peer less.
